finding.claim: The state-changing POST /settings/email route uses @login_optional instead of @login_required. An unauthenticated request reaches set_email with g.uid = None. Depending on set_email's behavior, this lets an anonymous caller change email on a null or unscoped account, or fail open. It is also a likely copy-paste misuse of the decorator, since the sibling /settings/password route uses login_required.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, an account email change (a precursor to account takeover via password reset)

trace.note: @login_optional applied, so no auth is enforced
g.uid = session.get('uid') evaluates to None for anonymous callers, and the wrapper calls f anyway

finding.guards_checked: Checked the login_required decorator (lines 8-16), which enforces a 401 but is not applied to this route. login_optional never aborts. The handler has no in-body check on g.uid. No other middleware or before_request hook exists in the file. The set_email stub is a no-op here, so the real impact depends on the production implementation.

verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") (None when anonymous) at routes.py:22 and never aborts, so an anonymous POST reaches set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37 with no in-handler check, unlike /settings/password at routes.py:42, which uses @login_required.
